etymology: Hebrew Chavvoth Yair, “the villages of Jair”; a group of towns in Gilead and Bashan taken and named by Jair the son of Manasseh.
biblical_def: Havoth-jair, “the villages of Jair,” was a cluster of towns in Gilead and Bashan seized and renamed by a mighty man of Manasseh: “And Jair the son of Manasseh went and took the small towns thereof, and called them Havothjair” (Num 32:41); and again, “Jair the son of Manasseh took all the country of Argob…and called them after his own name” (Deu 3:14). These towns lay in the rich pasture-land east of Jordan, part of the kingdom of Og that the LORD gave into Israel’s hand. The naming of the villages after Jair preaches the honour God grants to faithful valour. Jair was a man who went and took possession of what God had given, and his name was written upon the land for generations. Later a judge of Israel also named Jair had thirty sons who rode thirty ass colts and had thirty cities, called Havoth-jair unto this day. The villages of Jair witness that the LORD gives the land to those who will go up and possess it, and sets an honour upon them that are valiant for the inheritance. The people of God are called, like Jair, not to leave the promises unclaimed but to go in and take possession in the strength of the LORD, that His gift may not lie idle but be entered, held, and enjoyed to His glory.

etymology: Hebrew Geshur, perhaps “bridge”; a small Aramean kingdom on the border of Bashan, not driven out by Israel; the home of Absalom’s mother and his place of exile.
biblical_def: Geshur was a little Aramean kingdom on the north-eastern border of Bashan, among the peoples Israel failed to drive out: “Nevertheless the children of Israel expelled not the Geshurites, nor the Maachathites: but the Geshurites and the Maachathites dwell among the Israelites until this day” (Josh 13:13). This unfinished conquest bore bitter fruit generations later. David took to wife a princess of Geshur, Maacah, and she bore him Absalom; and when Absalom had slain his brother Amnon, “Absalom fled, and went to Geshur, and was there three years” (2Sa 13:38), taking refuge among his mother’s heathen kindred. From that unhallowed alliance and that half-hearted reconciliation grew the rebellion that nearly cost David his throne. Geshur preaches the long peril of a conquest left unfinished and a compromise with the world. What Israel spared came back to trouble her; what David joined himself to in Geshur returned in the person of Absalom to break his heart. The sin left un-mortified, the enemy left un-expelled, the alliance made with the ungodly — these do not stay quiet, but grow and return in judgment. The believer is warned to make no peace with the flesh, to leave no Canaanite in the land of the heart, but to put sin wholly to death, lest what is spared arise at last to his ruin.

etymology: Hebrew Argob, perhaps “region of clods” or “stony”; a region of Bashan containing threescore fenced cities of the kingdom of Og.
biblical_def: Argob was a region of Bashan, a country of many strong walled cities that belonged to the kingdom of Og and fell to Israel in the conquest: “And we took all his cities at that time, there was not a city which we took not from them, threescore cities, all the region of Argob, the kingdom of Og in Bashan” (Deu 3:4). Sixty fenced cities, with high walls, gates, and bars, besides many unwalled towns, made Argob a formidable land; yet the LORD delivered them all into Israel’s hand, for Og was the last of the remnant of the giants, and neither his stature nor his iron bedstead could save him. Argob, the land of threescore fenced cities all taken, preaches the completeness of God’s victory over the strongest strongholds. Not one city held out against the LORD when His hour was come; walls and giants alike fell before the people He led. So the weapons of the Christian’s warfare are mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds, casting down imaginations and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God. No fortress of sin or unbelief, however walled and manned, can stand when the LORD goes forth to give His people the victory; the region of the sixty cities was taken, and every high thing shall be brought low before Him.

etymology: Hebrew Salchah (Salcah), of uncertain meaning; a city at the far eastern edge of Bashan, marking the extent of Og’s kingdom.
biblical_def: Salcah was a city at the farthest eastern reach of Bashan, marking the limit of the kingdom of Og that the LORD gave to Israel: “All the cities of the plain, and all Gilead, and all Bashan, unto Salchah and Edrei, cities of the kingdom of Og in Bashan” (Deu 3:10); Og “reigned in mount Hermon, and in Salcah, and in all Bashan” (Josh 12:5). Salcah stood on the desert frontier, the boundary-stone of the eastern conquest. It preaches the fulness of what God gave. Israel received not a strip or a portion only, but all Bashan unto Salcah and Edrei, to the very edge; the LORD kept His word to the uttermost bound. He is a God who gives fully, not grudgingly; His promises reach to the farthest border, and He withholds no good thing from them that walk uprightly. As Israel possessed the land even unto Salcah, so the believer inherits all things in Christ, in whom are all the promises yea and amen; there is no half-salvation, no partial redemption. The God who gave Bashan to its farthest city gives His people the whole inheritance of grace, and will bring them to the uttermost bound of glory, having begun a good work and being faithful to perform it unto the day of Jesus Christ.

etymology: Hebrew Ashtaroth; a chief city of Bashan, the royal seat of Og; its name is that of the Canaanite goddess Ashtoreth, whose worship was there; distinct from the goddess herself.
biblical_def: Ashtaroth was a chief city of Bashan, the royal residence of Og the giant-king: “Og king of Bashan, which was at Ashtaroth” (Josh 9:10); he “dwelt at Astaroth in Edrei” (Deu 1:4). After Og was overthrown, the city fell to the half-tribe of Manasseh, to the children of Machir (Josh 13:31), and was afterward set apart as a Levitical city. This is a place, distinct from Ashtoreth the goddess — yet the city bore the goddess’s name, for it had been a centre of her foul worship, the worship of the queen of heaven with her groves and her shameful rites. That a city so named should become a possession of Israel and a Levitical city preaches the triumph of the LORD over the idols and the reclaiming of what was defiled for holy use. Where the name of Ashtoreth had been honoured, the Levites of the true God came to dwell. So the gospel takes ground once held by idols and plants there the worship of the living God; the strong holds of Satan are cast down, and the very places of abomination are cleansed and consecrated. The city of the goddess became a city of the Levites, a token that the LORD will have the victory over every false god and turn the seats of idolatry into dwellings of His truth.

etymology: Hebrew Tishbi; a place in Gilead, the home of Elijah the Tishbite, the prophet of fire.
biblical_def: Tishbe was a place in Gilead, known chiefly as the home of the greatest of the early prophets, for so he is named at his sudden appearing before Ahab: “And Elijah the Tishbite, who was of the inhabitants of Gilead, said unto Ahab, As the LORD God of Israel liveth, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word” (1Ki 17:1). Out of this obscure Gileadite town came the man who withstood the whole apostasy of Ahab and Jezebel, called down fire from heaven on Carmel, and turned the hearts of the people back to the LORD. Tishbe, unknown but for its son, preaches that God raises His mightiest instruments from hidden places. Elijah was of no priestly city, no royal line, but a plain man of the rough eastern hills, and the LORD made him a prophet of fire before whom kings trembled. God is not bound to the great and famous; He calls whom He will, from where He will, and clothes the man of an obscure town with power from on high. Tishbe reminds the church never to despise the day of small things, nor the plain and hidden places, for out of such the LORD brings forth His Elijahs, and by the weak and lowly overturns the pride of kings and the false worship of the age.

etymology: Hebrew Lo Debar, perhaps “no pasture” or “no thing”; a place in Gilead where Mephibosheth dwelt before David sent for him, and whence Machir supplied David.
biblical_def: Lo-debar was a place in Gilead, east of Jordan, whose name may mean “no pasture” or “nothing” — a barren-sounding name fit for the hiding-place of a forgotten man. There dwelt Mephibosheth, the lame son of Jonathan and grandson of Saul, in the house of Machir the son of Ammiel (2Sa 9:4), out of sight and out of favour, until David sought him out to show him the kindness of God for Jonathan’s sake and set him at the king’s own table. From the same Lodebar, Machir afterward came to succour David in his flight from Absalom (2Sa 17:27). Lo-debar, the place of “no pasture,” preaches the sovereign grace that seeks out the undeserving in their low estate. Mephibosheth, lame and hidden in a barren place, could plead no merit and expected no favour; yet the king sent for him and made him to eat bread continually as one of the king’s sons. So the grace of God finds the sinner in his Lo-debar, in the barren land of the fall, lame and helpless and undeserving, and brings him from the place of nothing to the table of the King, to eat the bread of children by the covenant kindness of God, for the sake of Another whom the King loved.

etymology: Hebrew Rogelim, perhaps “fullers” or “treaders (of the fuller’s trade)”; a town in Gilead, home of Barzillai the aged friend of David.
biblical_def: Rogelim was a town in Gilead, the home of Barzillai the Gileadite, that aged and wealthy man who stood by David in his darkest hour: “when David was come to Mahanaim…Barzillai the Gileadite of Rogelim” (2Sa 17:27) brought beds, food, and provision to the king and his weary company when they fled before Absalom. When the rebellion was crushed and David returned in triumph, he would have taken Barzillai to Jerusalem to feast at his table, but the old man, fourscore years, asked only to die in his own city by the grave of his father and mother, and sent his servant in his stead. Rogelim, the town of faithful Barzillai, preaches the beauty of loyal friendship and honourable old age. Barzillai served the king in the day of trouble, sought no reward, and desired at the last only to go home and rest with his fathers. His was the friendship that loveth at all times, and the brother born for adversity. The believer learns from Rogelim to be faithful to the Lord’s anointed in the day of adversity, to serve without seeking reward, and to look at the end not for the honours of this world but for the quiet rest of home, the city that hath foundations, where the faithful gather with their fathers in the presence of the King.

corruption_summary: A town in Gilead, home of faithful Barzillai; it recovers the beauty of loyal friendship in adversity and honourable old age content to rest at home.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. A Gileadite town raises no modern quarrel. Its honour is its son Barzillai, who stood by David in his flight and sought no reward.

The principle to recover is loyal friendship and honourable age. Barzillai served the king in the day of trouble, sought no recompense, and desired at the last only to go home and rest with his fathers. His was the friend that loveth at all times, the brother born for adversity. The believer learns to be faithful to the Lord’s anointed in adversity, to serve without seeking reward, and to look at the end for the quiet rest of home, the city that hath foundations.

etymology: Hebrew Elaleh, “God is ascending” or “whither God goeth up”; a town near Heshbon, built by the Reubenites, later a city of Moab.
biblical_def: Elealeh was a town in the good pasture-land east of Jordan, built (that is, rebuilt and fortified) by the tribe of Reuben near Heshbon: “And the children of Reuben built Heshbon, and Elealeh, and Kirjathaim” (Num 32:37). The country was excellent for cattle, and the children of Reuben and Gad, having much livestock, sought and received their inheritance there. Its name, “God is ascending” or “whither God goeth up,” is a lofty one. Yet in later days Elealeh passed again into the hand of Moab, and the prophets took up a lamentation over it: Heshbon and Elealeh cried, their voice heard even unto Jahaz, when the joy of the harvest and the shouting for the vintage were made to cease. The town preaches the danger of the choice made by sight. Reuben and Gad chose their portion east of Jordan for its rich pasture, before the whole land was subdued, cleaving to the border and the world; and that eastern country was the first to be overrun and carried captive. Elealeh, whose name spoke of God ascending, became a Moabite town and a byword of wailing. The believer is warned not to choose his portion by the seeing of the eyes, like Lot toward Sodom or Reuben toward the eastern pastures, but to seek first the kingdom, lest the fair choice of the flesh end in loss and lamentation.

etymology: Hebrew Baal Meon, “lord (Baal) of the dwelling”; a town near Heshbon built by Reuben, its name later changed; distinct from Baal the false god.
biblical_def: Baal-meon was a town near Heshbon, among those built by the tribe of Reuben in the land east of Jordan: “And Nebo, and Baalmeon, (their names being changed,) and Shibmah” (Num 32:38). The parenthesis is telling: the names of these towns were changed, for they bore the names of false gods — Nebo the Babylonian idol, and Baal in Baal-meon, “the lord of the dwelling.” This is a place, distinct from Baal the false god whose name it carried; and the changing of the names shows Israel’s duty to blot out the memory of the idols from the land. The people were commanded to destroy the places of the heathen worship and not so much as to take the names of their gods into their mouths. Baal-meon preaches the calling to purge idolatry root and branch, even from the speech and the map. Yet, like Elealeh and Nebo, Baal-meon fell back at last into heathen hands and is named in the prophets’ oracles against Moab. The town whose name meant “lord of the dwelling” reminds the believer that there can be but one Lord of the dwelling of the heart. Where Baal is named lord, the LORD is dethroned; and the soul must change the name of its dwelling, casting out the old lord and enthroning Christ, that its house may be the temple of the living God.
